To writers wringing their hands over how #MeToo “forces” them to write women differently:

Daniel Defoe’s MOLL FLANDERS is almost 300 years old. A woman character with wit, agency, and strong opinions about sexual harassment and assault is old hat. Where have you been?
#writing

Do some men feel that #MeToo challenges their identity? My generation grew up watching RAMBO and DIE HARD and INDIANA JONES. And I saw white boys invest in a self-image centered on violence. Violence which, as grown men, their race and gender privilege largely protects them from.

White men simply have more agency in when and how they encounter violence. For too many, it’s little more than a sport. #MeToo reveals reality. Learning that women, people of color, and LGBTQ+ folx experience more pervasive and intrusive violence must challenge that self-image.

Many white men have either been shocked at my appreciation of violent literature—or have nudged me toward women authors who don’t address violence. The underlying assumption is always that as a woman, I have less experience with violence. #MeToo shows the opposite to be true.

Many men and boys are victims of sexual assault and abuse as well. Our society pressures men to prove masculinity through silence and toughness, presenting these survivors with a host of obstacles to their healing. Follow @billydinkel @theunquiet1 @RAINN @MaleSurvivorORG #MeToo

“Two powerful men presided over an entrenched culture of misogyny, bullying and harassment” at Victoria’s Secret. It is perhaps unsurprising that men used women’s pleasure as an opportunity to exploit them—retaliating against any woman who said no. #MeToo  https://t.co/MI1UTWAVJW

Let’s talk about the physics of #assault. I’m a bantamweight. The average woman is a welterweight. The average man is a light heavyweight. Assault is often a power move, asserting that a physical disparity justifies entitlement to other bodies. #MeToo #PTSD #genderequity
